lessons.grammarFocus: Greet someone with bonjour and introduce yourself with je m’appelle. The j in je and bonjour sounds /ʒ/; ou in bonjour sounds /u/; on in bonjour is a nasal vowel /ɔ̃/ with no separate n sound. Some final consonants are silent (Paris, salut), but others are pronounced (Marc, Paul, bonjour). Use vous with an adult you have just met; save tu for familiar classmates once you agree to be informal. A woman writes enchantée with a final -e; it sounds the same as enchanté.

lessons.grammarFocus: French nouns are grammatically masculine or feminine. Learn each object with its article: un stylo, une trousse. Use un/une when naming or introducing one object (C’est un cahier); use le/la for a particular object already identified (Voilà la gomme). The noun ending is only a partial gender clue, so learn the article with the noun. Hear the difference between nasal un and pronounced n in une, and between le and la.

lessons.grammarFocus: Most French plurals are written with -s: un crayon → des crayons. The final -s is usually silent, so the article often tells you whether one or several are meant: le /lə/ versus les /le/, un or une versus des /de/. Un and une become des for unspecified plural objects; le and la become les for specific plural objects. Nouns already ending in -s, -x, or -z keep that ending in the plural. Other patterns come later; learn each new plural in context.

lessons.grammarFocus: Use être for “am / is / are”: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont. Peers often use tu right away; use vous with a teacher, staff member, or an adult stranger, and keep one register in a conversation. A mixed group uses ils, and masculine plural étudiants; an all-female group uses elles and étudiantes. In est the final t is usually silent, but it links before a vowel in il est ici; the t in êtes is pronounced.

lessons.grammarFocus: Use être for roles and traits: je suis étudiant or étudiante; il est gentil, elle est gentille. A role normally has no article after être: je suis étudiante. Learn the noun or adjective ending for the person described. Learn Je viens de as a fixed origin chunk for now: de France for a feminine country, d’Espagne before a vowel, du Canada for a masculine country, and des États-Unis for a plural country. Country articles matter; do not apply de to every country.

lessons.grammarFocus: Use être for the locations and states in this lesson: Le livre est sur la table; La porte est ouverte. Some other everyday states use avoir (for example, j’ai faim); those come later. Sur means on, dans means in, and près de means near; before le, de + le becomes du (près du livre), and before les it becomes des (here meaning de + les, distinct from the indefinite article des). For a thing, il replaces a masculine noun and elle a feminine noun: le livre → il, la trousse → elle. Adjectives agree with the noun or person: le livre est ouvert, la porte est ouverte; Marc est fatigué, Claire est fatiguée.

lessons.grammarFocus: Il y a means there is or there are and does not change for number. Use est, a form of être, for where a particular thing is. In il n’y a pas de + noun, de replaces un, une or des; write d’ before a vowel: il n’y a pas d’ordinateur. Review la/une/les with noun gender and number.

lessons.grammarFocus: French uses avoir for age: j’ai dix-huit ans, literally “I have eighteen years,” never je suis. Learn j’ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons; Tu as quel âge ? asks “How old are you?” Use il y a for a count and avoir besoin de + number + noun for a need. Count 1–20, including dix-huit and vingt. Pronunciation: dix is /dis/ alone, /di/ before a consonant, /diz/ before a vowel; dix-huit is /dizɥit/ and vingt ans links the final t. There is no elision before onze: de onze livres.

lessons.grammarFocus: Make a negative with ne before the verb and pas after it: je ne suis pas, je n’ai pas. Before a vowel or mute h, ne becomes n’: elle n’est pas, je n’ai pas. After a negated avoir, un/une/des usually become de: je n’ai pas de livre; after être, keep the article: ce n’est pas un livre. Ask yes/no questions with rising intonation (Tu as un livre ?) or est-ce que. In conversation ne is often dropped, but write the full ne…pas in this course. Être covers identity and location; avoir expresses possession. Je suis étudiant has no article before the role.

lessons.grammarFocus: New repair phrases: Je ne comprends pas (ce mot); Tu peux répéter, s’il te plaît ?; Plus lentement, s’il te plaît. Use Vous pouvez répéter, s’il vous plaît ? with a teacher. Comprendre means to understand; répéter means to repeat; plus lentement means more slowly. Review être, articles, noun/adjective agreement, il y a from Lesson 7, and full ne…pas. With a plain role, say je suis étudiante without an article; when the role noun has an adjective, the article returns: je suis une nouvelle étudiante or je suis un nouvel étudiant. The adjective comes before the noun: nouveau before a masculine consonant, nouvel before a masculine vowel sound (un nouvel étudiant), and nouvelle for feminine (une nouvelle étudiante). Plus has a silent s in plus lentement. Keep the pronoun/verb in the chosen tu or vous register. Pronunciation: un étudiant links the n to the vowel; est-ce que sounds roughly “es-kuh”; the final consonants of comprends and pas are silent; il y a is pronounced together as a short group.
